clue.text: Fail to make joke, say, for periodical

indicators.note: say tells the solver to speak the pieces and hear another word

parts.note: to fail is to DIE (as an engine dies) and to make a joke is to JEST; together, spoken, they give the noun's dye-jest pronunciation

explanation.surface: A comedian who cannot raise a laugh is sent off to write for a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The noun is stressed on its first syllable, DY-jest, which is what DIE + JEST says.
explanation.definitionFit: A digest is a magazine of condensed articles, as in Reader's Digest, so it is a kind of periodical.

indicators.note: regularly means take every other letter of the word Druid, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A druid keeps turning up and achieving nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dud is something that fails to work, so as an adjective it means useless or worthless.

parts.note: GEN is British slang for information
Eric Morecambe was half of the British comedy double act Morecambe and Wise

explanation.surface: A vague dossier on the seaside town of Morecambe.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe looks like the Lancashire resort, but it is the comedian Eric Morecambe, giving ERIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Generic means general, applying to a whole class rather than to any particular one.

clue.text: But it is actually the bookies' final offer

definitions.text: But it is actually the bookies' final offer

parts.words: But it is actually the bookies' final offer
parts.note: the phrase sounds like the opening price, yet it names the odds fixed as a race begins, the last a bookmaker gives

explanation.surface: A paradox: something called the start is really the end of a bookmaker's dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: In British horse-race betting the starting price is the official odds when the race starts, used to settle bets.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers' odds stop changing once the off is called, so the price at the start is the final one offered.

parts.note: IN means fashionable or popular
MATE is British slang for a friend

explanation.surface: A convict who gets on well with a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is a person confined in a prison or other institution.

clue.text: Of course, seasoned style is flowing

indicators.note: flowing suggests the letters of seasoned style run freely into a new order

explanation.surface: A seasoned writer's fluent prose, which naturally goes without saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Needless to say is an idiom meaning obviously, which is what of course conveys.

clue.text: Could you say flying is frightening?

definitions.meaning: a-wing is an old form meaning on the wing, in flight, and the question admits that this reading is a stretch
this sense means filling someone with awe or dread

explanation.surface: A wondering question about whether flight is scary.
explanation.walkthrough: A-WING (in flight, an old form) and AWING (inspiring awe) are written alike, so this is two definitions joined by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Awing means inspiring awe, an overwhelming dread or wonder, close to frightening, while a-wing means in flight.

parts.note: cushy means easy, undemanding
schooling is divided into TERMS, the periods of the school year

explanation.surface: A question of whether a soft education deserves praise.
explanation.walkthrough: Credit looks like praise, but it is buying now and paying later.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy terms are generous instalment arrangements, a form of buying on credit.

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: a NOD signals approval

explanation.surface: Someone gives a nod of approval concerning a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna is an Italian title for a lady and a common girl's name, so it stands for a girl.

parts.note: WEE is Scottish for small
PIES are snacks

explanation.surface: Little nibbles eaten in the cinema during a love story.
explanation.definitionFit: Weepies are sentimental films or stories made to bring tears, often romances.

clue.text: We must keep one little coin clean

indicators.note: must keep means the word We holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
P is a penny, the smallest British coin

explanation.surface: We have to hang on to one small coin, kept spotless.
explanation.definitionFit: To wipe something is to clean it by rubbing with a cloth.

indicators.note: detained by means the first letter is held inside the abbreviation

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A pupil kept in detention by the head teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools pupils address a male teacher as Sir.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir is the form of address used for a male schoolteacher, so it names one.

clue.text: Famous person to take lodgings right on the sea

parts.note: a STAR is a celebrity
BOARD is food and lodging, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: A celebrity takes rooms at a seaside hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: Starboard is the right-hand side of a ship as one faces forward, the sailor's term for right.

definitions.meaning: the ... of stairs leads up to the attic

explanation.surface: An estate agent's praise for the staircase up to the loft.
explanation.definitionFit: A top-flight performer is first-rate, in the highest division, hence excellent.

parts.note: a SCENT is a pleasant smell

explanation.surface: A lovely smell starts to waft upwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Rise looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a climb.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is a climb or upward movement, as a rise is.

indicators.note: seen in says the answer is visible inside the words vest here

explanation.surface: A girl glimpsed wearing a vest around here.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is a female first name, so it can stand for a girl.

clue.text: Top ten perhaps, the ones to be done away with?

definitions.meaning: a list of hit records, such as a chart's top ten

definitions.text: the ones to be done away with?
definitions.meaning: a ... names people targeted for killing

explanation.surface: A chart countdown that doubles as a gangster's list of targets.
explanation.definitionFit: A hit list can be a chart of popular songs or a list of people marked for murder.

indicators.note: read out means the word for questions is spoken, giving the answer's sound

parts.note: WHYS are questions, as in the whys and wherefores

explanation.surface: Reasonable queries spoken aloud at a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Wise means showing good judgement, which is what sensible means.

parts.note: BLUE means smutty or indecent, as a blue film
a PRINT is a photographic copy

explanation.surface: A request to produce a smutty picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Instruction to make is the definition, not an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A blueprint is a technical drawing or detailed plan from which something is built.

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A few handy customs suit a fanatic.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'for extremist' was changed to 'extremist': 'for' is a link word, and 'for extremist' cannot stand in for a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is a person holding extreme views, especially in politics or religion.

definitions.meaning: the contracted, poetic form of it is
TI is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A statement that something has been abbreviated in written jottings.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tis contracts it is; tis are several of the sol-fa note also spelt te.

clue.text: A long pace with one leg each side

parts.note: a STRIDE is a long step

explanation.surface: A walker's long step that leaves them straddling something.
explanation.definitionFit: Astride means sitting or standing with legs apart on either side of something, as on a horse.

clue.text: Am turning to leave dog? Tough

indicators.note: to leave means these letters go out of the dog's name

parts.note: a MASTIFF is a large breed of dog

indicators.note: turning means the word Am is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to turn away and abandon their dog, and finds it hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff means difficult or severe, as in a stiff test, which is a sense of tough.

clue.text: In favour of class losing marks

indicators.note: losing means a letter is dropped from the word for class

parts.note: a FORM is a school class in Britain
M is the standard abbreviation of the mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A school class that supports something after having its marks docked.
explanation.definitionFit: To be for something is to support it, which is to be in favour of it.

indicators.note: returned means the word for prize comes back, read from the end

parts.note: a REWARD is a prize

explanation.surface: A painter's award has been sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: Artist's is Artist is, the 's a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawer is someone who draws pictures, so an artist.

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the next piece
horrible suggests the letters of story are mangled into another order

explanation.surface: A gruesome tale about a European's dinner of shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horrible' turns STORY into OYSTR; 'about' puts it round E.
explanation.definitionFit: An oyster is a shellfish eaten as seafood.
